why: Each unit at city i protects either i or i - 1, so decisions only interact with the neighbouring city. Scanning left to right with a state 'is city i already protected by a unit that stayed' gives a two-state linear DP, a cousin of the week's greedy approach.
hints: A unit's choice only touches city i or i - 1. What small piece of information about the previous city do you need as you scan?

Keep two values: best total so far if the previous city is protected, and if it is not yet protected. A unit at i either moves left (protects i - 1, i stays unprotected for now) or stays (protects i).

Transitions per city in O(1); finalize city i - 1's population when you process unit i. O(n) time, O(1) space. Greedy alternative: in each block of consecutive units, all of them can shift left except that you drop the single smallest city.
pitfalls: The unit in the first city cannot move left.
Two units on the same city count its population once.
Moving left can leave the unit's own city unprotected; the DP must allow that, not just compare pairs greedily.
constraints:
• Numeric bounds are not stated in the source. Assume 1 <= n <= 10^5 and 1 <= population[i] <= 10^9.
  • unit.length == n and unit contains only '0' and '1'.
  • The total can exceed 32 bits, so return a 64-bit value.
